chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: The word 'swing' and the slang praising a good solo
summary: Asked what he called his music, Horace says 'swing' was used along with phrases like 'you stridin' tonight'; he first heard it in Fletcher's original band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Most of the time that we've been

talking, you've usually used the word swing in reference to your music. Did you ever call it anything else or, for instance, in -- well, we've used the term stride piano and so on, but has the term swing usually been the term that you've used to describe most of the music that you've played and Fletcher played? I mean, obviously, jazz, but as opposed to ragtime or dixieland or New Orleans?

Yeah, I think we used swing more As you were asking me this question, I was trying to figure right along with you than we did the other terms. ^ (Unintelligible). A lot of times the fellows in the band would use certain "crp" terms, as we'd call it. If a guy would get up and play a solo, he says, "Man, you really (Inaudible portion) played that 32, " Or he might use term "You stridin' tonight, man," or they may say some other tunes, we've tried in the band or even saying, "You got your tinish together tonight, man. You were kind of thing. Last night we did a little frail, you know. They would use those There were, all sort of expressions. They would still mean "You're the same thing as swing. We're swinging tonight, man. You really got that beat going, one of those things. (Unintelligible).
Can you recall perhaps where that term was first used? Do you have any idea? In your own vocabulary was it already in existence by the time you were playing jazz, or did it come in at a later time?

I think the first personnel in (unintelligible) Fletcher's original band used this a lot. This is where I first heard it, one of those things, you know. Of course, you you'd carry it quite a bit of that would rub off on me -- jazz (inaudible)

into your own group, and then these young guys would pick it up, young musicians would become hip. They would rub off on me. Then other musicians (unintelligible) would use those expressions, especially after you tell them guys like Louis Armstrong and Coleman Hawkins used it. They thought it was a big thing, you know.
